node.label: Emily S. Rosenberg
node.date_label: Spreading the American Dream (1982) · Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) · A World Connecting (2012, editor)
node.description: In Spreading the American Dream (1982), Emily S. Rosenberg traces how American economic and cultural expansion in the first half of the twentieth century evolved from a largely private system to an increasingly public one. Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) connects international lending and financial advising to claims of professional expertise and to ideas of gender, race and civilization; it received SHAFR’s Ferrell Senior Book award in 2000. Her later work examines contested Pearl Harbor memories and global networks. In the 2013 H-Diplo discussion of A World Connecting (2012), Erez Manela praised her synthesis but questioned its account of spatial differences and change over time; Donna R. Gabaccia asked for fuller integration of migration across the edited volume. Rosenberg defended uneven, interactive processes as an analytical framework. David A. Bell’s 2013 review likewise praised the research while criticizing weak causal explanation and the volume’s treatment of war.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Spreading the American Dream: American Economic and Cultural Expansion, 1890–1945 (1982); “Gender” (1990); Financial Missionaries to the World: The Politics and Culture of Dollar Diplomacy, 1900–1930 (1999); A Date Which Will Live: Pearl Harbor in American Memory (2003); A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012, editor and chapter author); Transnational Currents in a Shrinking World, 1870–1945 (2014 standalone issue of 2012 chapter); Body and Nation (2014, coeditor with Shanon Fitzpatrick).
node.scope_note: Spreading the American Dream read only in the publisher’s displayed opening excerpt. Financial Missionaries read in truncated chapter openings from the later Duke edition. Selected H-Diplo reviews and Rosenberg’s response, Bell’s review, institutional biographies and publisher descriptions read. Complete monographs, textbooks, “Gender,” and the Body and Nation chapters remain unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenberg and Gary Gerstle coauthored America Transformed: A History of the United States Since 1900 (1999), with Norman L. Rosenberg.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sidney Sussex profile, Book publications, entry beginning “America Transformed”; History Matters, “Forum on Immigration & Ethnicity,” confirms the three authors and 1999. Bibliographic collaboration only; no claim of shared authorship of every passage or intellectual dependence. Full textbook unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenberg and James M. McPherson were among the coauthors of Liberty, Equality, Power: A History of the American People (1996), alongside John Murrin, Paul Johnson, Gary Gerstle and Norman Rosenberg.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: History Matters, Gerstle’s November 1999 “Forum on Immigration & Ethnicity” biography, sentence listing “Liberty, Equality, Power” and its six coauthors; Rosenberg’s December 2000 biography corroborates her credit. Names refer to the historian James McPherson. Original textbook unread; no attribution of particular chapters.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2013 response about A World Connecting (2012), Rosenberg defends a global history of uneven interactions and argues that connection can generate exclusion and conflict.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo XIV.40, Rosenberg pp. 30–32, especially response to Foster and Manela; “relational, co-productive, and nonsynchronous change.” Her own response read; the book’s chapters remain unread. No universal theory of all globalization is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Financial Missionaries to the World (1999) examines U.S. lending and financial advising to less powerful nations, justified as extending 'civilization', and treats gender and race among the terms of that justification.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: JSTOR’s displayed opening of chapter 2, “The Roosevelt Corollary and the Dominican Model of 1905,” p. 31, names “race and manhood” among the conditions of dollar diplomacy; chapter 8 opening p. 219 names “masculine rationality.” Read in later Duke edition, copyright 2003. Full chapters and original 1999 edition unread; original date corroborated by Contemporary Authors.

proposed_edges.relationship: A Date Which Will Live: Pearl Harbor in American Memory (2003) examines competing public meanings of Pearl Harbor and their use in interpreting later events, including September 11.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke publisher description, three paragraphs beginning with the date of the attack; specifically names movies, memorials, public ceremonies and competing political uses. Description read; book and complete reviews unread. A contribution to historical memory research, not a claim to have originated the field.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Spreading the American Dream (1982), as Rosenberg describes it in “Doing History” (2020), she wrote an interpretive history of the ideology of ‘free flow’ that joined trade and investment to communications, movies and consumerism, organised the interpretation around ‘liberal developmentalism’, and widened ‘American diplomacy’ to foreign relations carried by private-sector actors.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, “The Ideology of Liberal-Developmentalism,” five-feature definition and concluding paragraphs on promotional, cooperative and regulatory states. Author expressly limits this account to expansion’s American promoters rather than a complete assessment of its effects on other societies. Excerpt read; rest of book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her H-Diplo essay “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg says that in her SHAFR presidential address, given after her election as president in 1997, she presented dollar diplomacy as part of a turn-of-the-century discourse of masculinity, “using discourse in the Foucauldian sense”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (19 February 2020), Rosenberg’s own reflective essay, read in full on issforum.org. (1) Paragraph beginning “The actors in the drama of dollar diplomacy”: “I used my presidential address to suggest how this dollar diplomacy emerged as part of a turn-of-the-century discourse of masculinity (using discourse in the Foucauldian sense).” (2) Paragraph beginning “I began attending SHAFR conventions”: her cohort wanted the field to consider “theories related to discourse (Michel Foucault)”, with n. 8 citing Foucault’s The Order of Things (English ed. 1970). This is a stated methodological debt in her own words, tied to a named piece of her work. Limits: the presidential address itself (published in Diplomatic History) was not read; no claim is made about which Foucault texts shaped it beyond n. 8, and the claim does not extend to Financial Missionaries (1999) as a whole.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg recalls that Akira Iriye, after reading Spreading the American Dream (1982), promoted and taught the book, later collaborated with her on Pearl Harbor memory and on A World Connecting (2012), and was “the most generous of mentors”.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (2020), paragraph beginning “Chance #5 emerged after Spreading was published”: “That would change after Akira Iriye read Spreading and, without ever having met me, began promoting the book in all kinds of ways. He assigned it for years to successive classes at Harvard”; “Iriye and I would collaborate on two projects— one on Pearl Harbor in historical memory (resulting in my book A Date Which Will Live, 2003) and one reconceptualizing World History”; “One of the most influential historians of his generation, he was also the most generous of mentors.” A stated mentorship and collaboration in her own words. Same pair as the verified esr_w_02 (Iriye as general editor of the History of the World series), but a distinct and stronger claim; the coordinator may keep both, or fold esr_w_02 into this edge. It adds no new distinct partner. Rosenberg also says they “worked on parallel tracks” on cultural themes; no transfer of a specific argument is claimed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Iriye as promoter, collaborator and mentor

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Doing History” (2020), Rosenberg says she gravitated in graduate school toward the New Left’s Wisconsin School of diplomatic history, identified centrally with its open-door interpretation, and built the thesis of Spreading the American Dream (1982) heavily on William Appleman Williams’s The Tragedy of American Diplomacy.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Essay 195 (2020). Paragraph beginning “The field of U.S. diplomatic history was, at that time, polarized”: “the so-called Wisconsin School of New Left historians (Williams A Williams, Walter LaFeber, Lloyd Gardner, and others)”; “I gravitated toward the New Left”; her “true academic mentors” were Williams, LaFeber, Barnet, Kolko and Marilyn Young (n. 2: “Especially influential were” Williams, Tragedy; LaFeber, New Empire; Barnet; Young). Paragraph beginning “With small children at home”, on Spreading: “Based on my own research, I now identified centrally with that position” (the open door); “This thesis leaned heavily on William A. Williams’s Tragedy of American Diplomacy, but bringing in the dimension of America’s enormous cultural influence”. The graph node newleft covers radical diplomatic history. None of the named Wisconsin School historians is an endpoint, so the debt is recorded as a field relationship, not a person edge. Self-description; the book itself remains unread beyond the original packet’s publisher excerpt.
proposed_edges.map_label: Wisconsin School open door, extended to culture

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘How to Remember Pearl Harbor’ (2010), Mary L. Dudziak draws on Emily S. Rosenberg’s A Date Which Will Live: Pearl Harbor in American Memory (2003) to explain how remembering Pearl Harbor as the war’s beginning framed American military action as defensive, within Dudziak’s argument about the boundaries of wartime.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Dudziak’s complete signed post on the blog where she published it, dated 6 December 2010. Two successive body paragraphs explicitly attribute the interpretation to Rosenberg; the first links to her book. Dudziak connects that interpretation with her own argument about war powers and the temporal framing of World War II. The closing note identifies the post as drawn from an in-progress chapter; this edge concerns the published 2010 post, not an unread final book. Duke University Press’s book page confirms Rosenberg’s title and original August 2003 publication. No supervision or general career influence is claimed.
proposed_edges.map_label: Pearl Harbor memory in Dudziak’s wartime argument

proposed_edges.relationship: In her introduction to Haunted by Empire (2006), editor Ann Laura Stoler summarizes Emily S. Rosenberg’s chapter ‘Ordering Others: U.S. Financial Advisers in the Early Twentieth Century’ as showing that circuits of knowledge production are remade by the individuals who travel them.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed preview’s preface and introductory chapter, especially printed pp. 16–18. On p. 18 Stoler names Rosenberg, explains her examination of financial advisers and imperial practices, and uses it to develop the account of knowledge circuits. The contents identify Rosenberg’s essay at p. 405; its body is outside this preview and remains unread. This is a narrow claim about Stoler’s explicit editorial engagement, not evidence that Rosenberg originated Stoler’s broader framework. Conservatively excluded from the floor under the editor–contributor ruling. Duke’s publisher page confirms the volume’s 2006 publication and sole volume editor, Stoler.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenberg’s contribution to A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012) brought histories of science into an integrated account with technology and culture, an achievement singled out by Michael Goebel’s 2013 review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the original English review on H-Soz-Kult. Goebel identifies Rosenberg’s own contribution, rather than attributing every chapter of the edited volume to her, and expressly praises its integration of these histories. He also finds its conclusion banal; this proposal preserves that qualification and makes no claim of unqualified acclaim or disciplinary founding. The review identifies the book’s original year as 2012. The chapter itself remains unread. Only one field edge is proposed for this integrated achievement.
proposed_edges.map_label: Science linked with technology and culture
